appraisal_events.evidence: « Mais je n'osais pas le faire pour deux raisons »; « J'avais peur que Gilberte ne trouvât cela commun et n'en conçût un grand mépris pour nous »; « une difficulté de protocole que je ne pus jamais réussir à lever »; « un point qui me semblait plus grave qu'à la cour de Louis XIV le " Monseigneur " ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The remembering narrator diminishes his younger self by showing him paralyzed before the Swann household's usages, unable to act on a permission already granted, and inflating a question of tea, chocolate, and a polite formula into a matter of court protocol; the Louis XIV comparison is the retrospective irony that makes the deference itself the object of judgment.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Mais maman ne voulut rien entendre. — Mais non, puisque je ne connais pas Mme Swann. — Mais elle ne te connaît pas davantage. »
appraisal_events.explanation: The mother flatly refuses to return the courtesy Mme Swann extends to her, withholding the social recognition that the formula « Comment va Madame votre mère ? » would imply; the narrator's unanswered retort shows the stated reason is a pretext, since non-acquaintance has not stopped Mme Swann.

status_effects.explanation: He ends the passage locally weaker: dependent on the Swann household's approval, afraid of Gilberte's contempt, and blocked from an invitation he was already free to make.
She holds her ground without negotiating — « ne voulut rien entendre » — and closes off her son's repeated overtures with a single unmoved answer.
Her politeness is not reciprocated: the narrator's mother declines to acknowledge her as someone she knows, denying the Swann household the recognition it offers.

ambiguities: The mother's « puisque je ne connais pas Mme Swann » can be read as a plain statement of fact rather than as a refusal of recognition; it is annotated as a snub because the narrator's immediate rejoinder « Mais elle ne te connaît pas davantage » exposes the reason as a pretext, but the passage stops before she answers, so the text does not settle whether the refusal is principled or merely obstinate.

The contempt feared over the chocolate is given in free indirect style by the remembering narrator, so it is undetermined whether it reflects any disposition of Gilberte's or is entirely the child's projection; it is therefore recorded as the narrator's self-diminishment and not as an appraisal act by Gilberte.
